lesson.title: Why Reactions Actually Happen: The Driving Force Behind Chemical Change
lesson.summary: Reactions proceed toward products, rather than stalling as a mixture of reactants and products, when something removes a product from the system or releases energy, and recognizing these driving forces explains why some reactions go essentially to completion while others barely happen at all.
lesson.body:
The reaction types overview classified reactions into families such as synthesis, decomposition, single replacement, double replacement, and combustion, but knowing which family a reaction belongs to says nothing about whether it will actually happen, or happen all the way. Two substances can be mixed in a beaker and simply sit there as an unremarkable solution of ions, or they can react vigorously and essentially completely. What separates those outcomes is the driving force of the reaction: some feature of the products that makes the forward direction strongly favored over the reverse.

For reactions happening in aqueous solution, three driving forces show up again and again. The first is the formation of an insoluble solid, a precipitate, which physically leaves the solution and can no longer participate in the reverse reaction. The second is the formation of a gas that escapes the reaction vessel, again removing material from the system permanently. The third is the formation of a very stable, weakly ionizing molecule, most commonly water itself, which locks ions together into a form that strongly resists breaking back apart. These three, precipitate formation, gas formation, and water or weak-electrolyte formation, are precisely the driving forces that make double-replacement reactions proceed, the subject of the next chapter on metathesis reactions.

Beyond removing a product from the system, there is a second, more general driving force rooted in energy. Recall from the concept of energy that a system tends toward lower potential energy, and a reaction that releases energy to its surroundings, an exothermic reaction, converts some of the chemical potential energy stored in the reactants into heat, leaving the products at lower energy and making that direction thermodynamically favorable. Informally, you can think of any of these driving forces the same way: whenever something keeps pulling material or energy out of the reacting system, the reverse reaction has less and less chance to reassemble the original reactants, so the reaction keeps moving forward until a reactant is used up. This is exactly why chemists describe such reactions as going to completion, rather than settling into a persistent mixture of reactants and products.

Here is a worked numeric example showing the energy driving force in action. Suppose a student mixes 50.0 mL of 1.00 M HCl with 50.0 mL of 1.00 M NaOH in an insulated cup, and the temperature of the resulting 100.0 mL of solution rises from 22.00 degrees Celsius to 28.85 degrees Celsius. Using q = mcDeltaT, with mass approximated as 100.0 g (assuming a solution density close to 1.00 g/mL) and a specific heat of 4.18 J per gram per degree Celsius, the heat released is q = (100.0 g)(4.18 J/g degree C)(6.85 degree C) = 2863 J, or 2.86 kJ. The moles of acid that reacted equal (0.0500 L)(1.00 mol/L) = 0.0500 mol. Dividing heat released by moles reacted gives 2863 J divided by 0.0500 mol, which equals about 57,300 J per mole, or negative 57.3 kJ per mol since the energy is released. That value lines up closely with the commonly cited value of roughly negative 57 kJ per mole for the neutralization of any strong acid by any strong base, which makes sense because the actual reacting species in every such neutralization is the same net ionic pair, H+(aq) plus OH-(aq) forming H2O(l).

Over the next several chapters you will see these driving forces at work in specific reaction families: metathesis reactions driven by precipitate, gas, or water formation, acid-metal reactions driven by the formation of stable hydrogen gas alongside a favorable transfer of electrons, and disproportionation reactions driven by the greater overall stability of two new oxidation states compared to the single starting oxidation state.
